core_semantic_distinctions.meaning: The source contrasts physical chemistry's predominantly supramolecular/bulk orientation with chemical physics; the boundary is explicitly non-absolute ('predominantly, but not always').
Physical chemistry spans both macroscopic and microscopic chemical phenomena.
Chemical thermodynamics addresses what is possible/spontaneous and limits extent/energy conversion; chemical kinetics addresses whether/how fast reactions occur.
Classical thermodynamics primarily treats equilibrium and reversible changes; quasi-equilibrium/non-equilibrium thermodynamics provide limited descriptions of irreversible changes.
Statistical mechanics explains why very large molecular populations can often be represented by a small set of macroscopic variables.
Quantum chemistry describes structural/electronic features and nuclear motion; kinetics describes reaction pathways and rates.
Physical chemistry is framed as applying general physics to chemical problems rather than being detached from chemical systems.

claims.statement: Physical chemistry studies macroscopic and microscopic phenomena in chemical systems using physics concepts.
Physical chemistry is predominantly, but not always, supramolecular and bulk-oriented in contrast with chemical physics.

The field seeks relationships involving intermolecular forces, kinetics, ions/conductivity, surfaces/electrochemistry, heat/work, thermochemistry, colligative properties, phase rule, electrochemical cells, statistical thermodynamics, and electron-motion energies.
Physical chemistry applies pure physics to chemical problems.

Chemical compounds are described as groups of bonded atoms; reactions involve making/breaking bonds; predicting properties from atomic structure/bonding is a major goal; nuclei positions and electron distributions are needed for precision.
Quantum chemistry applies quantum mechanics to chemical problems and provides tools for bond strength/shape, nuclear motion, and absorption/emission.
Spectroscopy concerns interaction of electromagnetic radiation with matter.

Chemical thermodynamics studies spontaneity and mixture properties, limits reaction extent and energy conversion, links thermodynamic derivatives, assesses feasibility and validates experimental data, and has limited quasi-/non-equilibrium applications.
Classical thermodynamics mainly concerns equilibrium systems and reversible changes, not actual behavior or rates far from equilibrium.

Chemical kinetics studies which reactions occur and how fast; transition states are higher-energy barriers; higher barriers generally imply slower reaction; reactions often consist of elementary steps; rate depends on temperature, concentrations, catalysts and conditions.

Large particle populations can often be described with a few variables such as pressure, temperature and concentration; statistical mechanics explains why and predicts macroscopic properties from molecular properties without empirical chemical-similarity correlations.
Lomonosov coined the term physical chemistry in 1752 and taught a course titled A Course in True Physical Chemistry.

Modern physical chemistry originated in the 1860s–1880s around chemical thermodynamics, electrolytes, kinetics and related work; Gibbs's 1876 paper was a milestone introducing Gibbs energy, chemical potentials and Gibbs phase rule.

The first scientific journal specifically in physical chemistry was Zeitschrift für Physikalische Chemie, founded in 1887 by Ostwald and van 't Hoff; Ostwald, van 't Hoff and Arrhenius were leading figures and all won Nobel Prizes in Chemistry between 1901 and 1909.

Later developments included statistical mechanics applied to chemistry, colloids and surface chemistry, Langmuir's contributions, quantum chemistry from the 1930s, and spectroscopy developments including IR, microwave, EPR and NMR.
Further development included nuclear chemistry/isotope separation, astrochemistry, and computational methods for additive physicochemical properties.
The source names group contribution, Lydersen, Joback, Benson group increment theory, and QSAR.
The source lists physical chemistry journals and historical chemistry/physics journals.

The source lists chemical thermodynamics, kinetics, statistical mechanics, quantum chemistry, ion chemistry, microwave chemistry, electrochemistry, photochemistry, surface chemistry, solid-state chemistry, spectroscopy, biophysical chemistry, materials science, physical organic chemistry and micromeritics.
The source provides books, papers and historical works supporting the field.

nodes.label: Physical chemistry
nodes.definition: Study of macroscopic and microscopic phenomena in chemical systems using principles, practices, and concepts of physics.

nodes.label: Chemical physics
nodes.definition: Neighboring field contrasted with physical chemistry; the source characterizes physical chemistry as predominantly supramolecular/bulk-oriented rather than exclusively molecular or atomic.
nodes.distinction: Contrast category used to delimit scope; not presented as an absolute boundary.

nodes.label: Supramolecular / bulk-oriented science
nodes.definition: Scale/orientation emphasized for physical chemistry: many foundational principles concern bulk matter rather than molecular or atomic structure alone.

nodes.label: Principles of physics applied to chemistry
Quantum chemistry
nodes.definition: Subfield applying quantum mechanics to chemical problems; used to determine bond strength/shape, nuclear motion, and radiation absorption/emission.

nodes.label: Statistical mechanics
nodes.definition: Framework connecting microscopic properties and dynamics with macroscopic observables using statistical descriptions.

nodes.label: Thermochemistry
nodes.definition: Study of heat transfer between a chemical system and surroundings during phase changes or chemical reactions.

nodes.label: Phase rule
nodes.definition: Framework correlating number of phases, number of components, and degree of freedom/variance.

nodes.label: Colligative properties
nodes.definition: Properties of solutions depending on the number of species present.

nodes.label: Spectroscopy
nodes.definition: Sub-discipline concerned specifically with interaction of electromagnetic radiation with matter.

nodes.label: Transition state
nodes.definition: Higher-energy state/barrier configuration through which reacting species generally pass on the way from reactants to products.

nodes.label: Reaction mechanism
nodes.definition: Sequence of elementary reactions describing a chemical reaction pathway.
